subject: ENG
label: Grade 02
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 02 English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 8 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Phonics set 2 and spelling patterns
modules.outcome: read and spell words with common vowel pairs and blends
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Phonics set 2 and spelling patterns', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: read and spell words with common vowel pairs and blends. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Phonics set 2 and spelling patterns' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read and spell words with common vowel pairs and blends, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 3, 7, 11, 15: add 4 each time, so next is 19. The nth term is 4n - 1; check n = 4: 15. Method: Model run for 'Phonics set 2 and spelling patterns'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Read and spell words with common vowel pairs and blends: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Learn vowel pairs as sound teams. ai and ay say "ay": rain, tray. ee and ea say "ee": feet, leaf. oa says "oh": boat. Sort words by the sound, then check the spelling. Reason: a pair shares one sound.
Step 2, Choose ai or ay by position. Use "ai" in the middle of a word (rain, paint) and "ay" at the end (play, day). Model: "We play in the rain." Reason: English words rarely end in "ai".
Step 3, Read and spell blends. Blends: st, bl, cr, tr, sp. Word: "stamp" = s-t-a-m-p. Say the first two sounds quickly, then the vowel, then the end. Spell "crab": c-r-a-b.
Step 4, Fix an error. A child spells "boat" as "bote" or "rain" as "rane". Correction: bo-a-t uses the vowel pair oa, and r-ai-n uses ai. Say the word, tap the sounds, and write the pair together.
Step 5, Spell with the "say, tap, write" method. Word: "green". Say it, tap g-r-ee-n (four sounds), and write it. Check: the ee pair is two letters for one sound. Cover and write it again.
Step 6, Write a sentence using three pattern words. "The goat sat in the rain by the green tree." Pattern words: goat (oa), rain (ai), green (ee). Check spelling of each pair.
Step 7, Your turn. Spell these as you hear them: tray, leaf, coat. Model answer: t-r-ay, l-ea-f, c-oa-t. Then write one sentence: "I put my coat on the tray."

modules.title: Reading short passages
modules.outcome: read a short passage aloud and answer who, what, where questions
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Reading short passages', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: read a short passage aloud and answer who, what, where questions. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Reading short passages' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read a short passage aloud and answer who, what, where questions, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Passage: 'Ravi has a red kite. He flies it on the hill.' Who? Ravi. What? A red kite. Where? On the hill. Method: Model run for 'Reading short passages'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Read a short passage aloud and answer who, what, where questions: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Read for sense. Passage: "Tom has a red kite. He flies it in the park on Sunday. His sister Mia helps him." Read aloud smoothly, pausing at each full stop. Reason: stops give breath and meaning.
Step 2, Answer a who question. "Who has a kite?" Answer: "Tom has a kite." Find the name in the text and give a complete sentence. Reason: who asks about a person.
Step 3, Answer a what and where question. "What does Tom fly?" "He flies a red kite." "Where does he fly it?" "In the park." Reason: what asks about a thing; where asks for a place.
Step 4, Use the text to check. Question: "When does Tom fly the kite?" Answer: "On Sunday." Point to the words in the passage. Reason: the answer must come from the text, not from a guess.
Step 5, Fix an error. Question: "Who helps Tom?" Wrong answer: "The park." Right: "His sister Mia helps him." A who question needs a person. Read the question word first before you answer.
Step 6, Read with expression. A question ends with a rising voice: "Can you fly the kite?" An exclamation is stronger: "It is high!" Reason: punctuation tells you how to read.
Step 7, Your turn. Passage: "Ben has a cat. It sleeps on a mat by the door." Answer: Who has a cat? Where does it sleep? Model answer: "Ben has a cat." "It sleeps on a mat by the door."

modules.title: Nouns, common and proper
modules.outcome: tell common nouns from names that need capital letters
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Nouns, common and proper', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: tell common nouns from names that need capital letters. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Nouns, common and proper' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: tell common nouns from names that need capital letters, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: In 'Mira has a dog called Bruno', 'dog' is a common noun, 'Mira' and 'Bruno' are proper nouns and need capital letters. Method: Model run for 'Nouns, common and proper'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Tell common nouns from names that need capital letters: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Tell common from proper nouns. Common nouns name any one of a kind: girl, city, river. Proper nouns name a particular one: Sara, Lahore, Nile. Proper nouns begin with capital letters. Reason: they are special names.
Step 2, Sort a list. Words: boy, Omar, school, Green Hill School, dog, Rex. Common: boy, school, dog. Proper: Omar, Green Hill School, Rex. Reason: "dog" is any dog, "Rex" is one dog.
Step 3, Fix capital letters in a sentence. Wrong: "my friend aisha lives in karachi." Right: "My friend Aisha lives in Karachi." Capitals: the first word, the name Aisha, and the city Karachi.
Step 4, Capitalise days and months. Model: "On Monday in March we visit Cairo." Days, months and place names are proper nouns. But seasons are common: "We visit in spring."
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "We went to the Park with Our Dog." Right: "We went to the park with our dog." Only proper names get capitals. If the dog was named Max: "with our dog Max."
Step 6, Write a sentence with both. "The teacher, Mr Khan, gave a book to the girl." Common: teacher, book, girl. Proper: Mr Khan. Reason: the title and name together are one proper noun.
Step 7, Your turn. Rewrite with correct capitals: "last tuesday zara and her dog bruno went to the river." Model answer: "Last Tuesday Zara and her dog Bruno went to the river."

modules.title: Verbs and describing words
modules.outcome: use verbs and adjectives to make a sentence richer
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Verbs and describing words', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: use verbs and adjectives to make a sentence richer. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Verbs and describing words' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: use verbs and adjectives to make a sentence richer, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 'The girl runs.' Add describing words: 'The tall girl runs fast.' Tense: walk, walked, will walk. Method: Model run for 'Verbs and describing words'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Use verbs and adjectives to make a sentence richer: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Start with a plain sentence. "The dog barked." Add an adjective: "The big dog barked." Add a stronger verb: "The big dog howled." Reason: adjectives describe nouns and verbs show the action.
Step 2, Choose strong verbs. Plain: "walk". Stronger: "stroll", "stride", "creep", depending on the meaning. Model: "The cat crept across the floor." Reason: a precise verb paints a clearer picture.

Step 3, Choose adjectives that tell more than "nice". Instead of "a nice day", write "a bright, warm day". Use a comma between two adjectives of equal weight. Reason: precise adjectives give sensory details.
Step 4, Add where and when. "Yesterday the big dog howled loudly at the gate." Added: when (yesterday), how (loudly), where (at the gate). Reason: each detail answers a question the reader may ask.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "The more big dog ran fast." Right: "The bigger dog ran fast." Another weak sentence: "The boy went." Better: "The tired boy trudged home."
Step 6, Build a richer sentence from a simple one. Simple: "The bird sang." Richer: "The tiny red bird sang sweetly in the old tree." Underline verbs and adjectives to check you used both.
Step 7, Your turn. Make "The girl ran" richer with two adjectives and one stronger verb. Model answer: "The brave little girl raced down the dusty road."

modules.title: Poems and rhymes
modules.outcome: read, recite and make a short rhyming poem
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Poems and rhymes', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: read, recite and make a short rhyming poem. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read, recite and make a short rhyming poem, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: cat, hat and mat rhyme. Make a couplet: 'The sun is high, a bird can fly.' High and fly rhyme. Method: Model run for 'Poems and rhymes'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Read, recite and make a short rhyming poem: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Notice the rhyme. Poem lines (my own): "The cat sat down on the warm red mat, / and watched a small bird, plump and fat." Rhyming words: mat and fat. Reason: the end sounds match.
Step 2, Read the poem with rhythm. Clap the beats: "The CAT sat DOWN on the WARM red MAT." Reason: reading with a steady beat shows the rhythm of the poem.
Step 3, Recite from memory by learning one line at a time. Say line one three times, add line two, then say both. Use gestures. Reason: small steps and actions help the memory.
Step 4, Find rhyming words for your poem. Pick "sun": run, fun, bun. Pick "light": night, bright, kite. Check that the end sounds match, even if the spelling differs ("blue" and "too").
Step 5, Write two lines. "I see a bright and shining star, / It twinkles from so far." Check: "star" and "far" rhyme, and the lines have a similar length.
Step 6, Fix an error. Wrong: "I like my dog, / he likes to play on the log, / and then he sleeps all day." The last line is long and has no rhyme. Right: "and then he curls up like a frog."
Step 7, Your turn. Finish this couplet with a rhyming word and explain the rhyme. "I put on my boot / and ran to the..." Model answer: "fruit" (boot and fruit rhyme: both end with the "oot" sound).

modules.title: Speaking and listening
modules.outcome: retell, ask questions and respond politely
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Speaking and listening', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: retell, ask questions and respond politely. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Speaking and listening' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: retell, ask questions and respond politely, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Retell in order with first, next, then, last. Ask: 'What happened next?' Reply politely: 'Thank you, I agree because...' Method: Model run for 'Speaking and listening'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Retell, ask questions and respond politely: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Retell a short story in order. Story: "Dina lost her ball. She asked her friend. Her friend found it under the bench." Retell: "First Dina lost her ball. Then she asked her friend. At last it was found under the bench."
Step 2, Ask questions using who, what, where, why. "Who found the ball?" "Where did the friend find it?" "Why did Dina ask her friend?" Reason: question words show what kind of answer you need.
Step 3, Give a polite response. "Thank you for telling me." "That is a good idea." "I did not know that." Reason: a polite reply shows you listened.
Step 4, Listen then speak. Speaker: "I went to the market and bought a mango." Listener: "What colour was the mango?" Reason: a related question shows you were listening.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong response: "That is boring." Better: "I like the part about the market. Can you tell me more?" Another error: interrupting. Correction: wait until the speaker finishes, then speak.
Step 6, Use a complete sentence and a polite voice. "Please can I ask a question?" "Yes, go ahead." Reason: "please" and "thank you" make a conversation friendly.

Step 7, Your turn. Listen to: "I have a rabbit called Snow. It eats carrots." Ask one question and make one polite reply. Model answer: "What colour is Snow?" "That is a lovely name, thank you for telling me."

'read', at the Remember level.

ladder: L1: say and read familiar words and short sentences.
L2: read short texts and write connected sentences.
L3: write paragraphs and speak on a topic with notes.
L4: write for different purposes and analyse how texts persuade.
L5: write and argue at length; handle unseen texts.
L6 (degree): academic reading, writing and citation.
L7 (postgraduate): publish, teach or translate with expert accuracy.
